RC01.p:
(1) Sunlight carries more than visible light and warmth. It also carries ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which cannot be seen or felt but can still harm the skin. Two kinds of UV reach the ground. UVB rays have shorter wavelengths and cause most sunburns. UVA rays have longer wavelengths, travel deeper into the skin, and contribute to wrinkles and other signs of aging. Both kinds can contribute to skin cancer, so dermatologists urge people to protect their skin even on days when they do not burn.

(2) The number on a sunscreen bottle, the sun protection factor (SPF), measures protection against UVB. That number is easy to misread. An SPF 15 product blocks about 93 percent of UVB rays, SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent, and SPF 50 blocks about 98 percent. Doubling the number, in other words, does not double the protection, and no product blocks every ray. Because SPF says nothing about UVA, shoppers should also look for the words "broad spectrum," which mean a product has passed a test for UVA protection as well.

(3) Even a high SPF works only as well as it is applied. In laboratory tests, sunscreen is spread much more thickly than most people spread it at home; an adult covering the whole body needs about one ounce, roughly enough to fill a shot glass. Sunscreen also wears off. Swimming, sweating and toweling remove it, so guidelines call for reapplying at least every two hours and right after swimming. Products labeled "water resistant" must state whether they stay effective for 40 or 80 minutes in water; none is waterproof.

(4) Weather can mislead people, too. Up to 80 percent of UV rays pass through clouds, so a gray summer afternoon can still produce a painful burn. Snow, sand and water reflect UV back toward the skin, raising the exposure of skiers and beachgoers.

(5) For these reasons, sunscreen works best as one layer of protection rather than the only one. Shade, wide-brimmed hats, sunglasses and tightly woven clothing block rays without needing to be reapplied. Used correctly and together, these habits greatly reduce the dose of UV that reaches the skin.

RC02.t: A Map, a Pump and an Outbreak
RC02.p:
(1) In late August 1854, cholera swept through Soho, a crowded neighborhood in London. Within about ten days, more than 500 people living near Broad Street had died. Cholera causes severe diarrhea and can kill through dehydration in a matter of hours. At the time, most physicians believed that it spread through "miasma," a foul-smelling air thought to rise from rotting waste.

(2) John Snow, a London physician, doubted the miasma theory. During an earlier epidemic, he had noticed that cholera attacked the gut rather than the lungs, which suggested to him that people swallowed the cause rather than breathed it in. When the Soho outbreak began, he collected the addresses of people who had died and marked each death on a street map. The marks clustered tightly around a public water pump on Broad Street.

(3) The exceptions were just as revealing. A workhouse near the pump, home to more than 500 people, had its own well and recorded very few deaths. None of the workers at a nearby brewery, who received a daily allowance of beer, was reported to have died. Meanwhile, a widow who lived miles away in another district died of cholera after water from the Broad Street pump, whose taste she preferred, was carried to her home.

(4) On September 7, Snow presented his evidence to local officials. The next day, they ordered the handle removed from the pump so that no one could draw water from it. Deaths fell soon afterward, although Snow himself acknowledged that the outbreak had already been slowing, partly because many residents had fled the area.

(5) Snow's explanation was not widely accepted at first, and the pump handle was later put back. Further investigation eventually found that a leaking cesspool only a few feet from the well had most likely contaminated the water. Today, Snow's careful mapping, and his attention to the cases that did not fit the pattern, are often cited as an early model for how public health investigators trace the source of an outbreak.

RC03.p:
(1) When a patient in an emergency department struggles to breathe, one of the first people at the bedside is often a respiratory therapist. These licensed health professionals specialize in the lungs and airways. They care for premature infants whose lungs are not fully developed, older adults with chronic lung disease, and patients of every age who are recovering from surgery, injury or severe infection.

(2) Much of a respiratory therapist's day centers on assessment. Therapists listen to breath sounds, use pulmonary function tests to measure how much air a patient can move in and out, and draw blood from an artery to check its levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide. They share these findings with physicians and nurses, who use them to adjust each patient's plan of care.

(3) Therapists also deliver treatment. They give inhaled medications through nebulizers and inhalers, set up oxygen equipment, and teach exercises that help clear mucus from the airways. In intensive care units, they manage mechanical ventilators, machines that breathe for patients who cannot breathe adequately on their own. Because small changes in a ventilator's settings can affect a patient's oxygen level within minutes, therapists check these patients often.

(4) Teaching is a quieter but equally important part of the job. A therapist may spend twenty minutes showing a child with asthma how to use a spacer with an inhaler, or coaching an adult with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in breathing techniques that ease shortness of breath at home. Patients who understand their treatment are better prepared to manage their symptoms between visits.

(5) Entering the field requires at least an associate degree from an accredited program, followed by a national credentialing exam, and nearly every state also requires a license. Many therapists later earn a bachelor's degree or specialize in areas such as newborn care or sleep medicine. For applicants who want direct patient contact, technical skill and teamwork in one career, respiratory therapy offers all three.

RC04.p:
(1) For many adults, the day does not really begin until the first cup of coffee. Caffeine is the most widely used stimulant in the world, found in coffee, tea, many soft drinks, energy drinks and even chocolate. Its effects feel simple: more alertness and less fatigue. The chemistry behind them, and the reason an afternoon latte can disturb sleep many hours later, is less obvious.

(2) Throughout the waking day, a compound called adenosine builds up in the brain. As adenosine attaches to receptors on brain cells, it slows their activity and produces a growing feeling of sleepiness, sometimes called sleep pressure. Caffeine's shape is similar enough to adenosine's that it can occupy those same receptors without activating them. With the receptors blocked, the brain receives a weaker sleepiness signal, so a person feels more awake. The adenosine does not disappear, however. As the caffeine wears off, the sleep pressure that built up in the meantime can return all at once.

(3) How long caffeine lasts depends on how quickly the body clears it. In healthy adults, its half-life, the time the body needs to remove half of a dose, averages about five hours, although it ranges from roughly two to more than ten hours from one person to another. Pregnancy and some medications slow its breakdown, while smoking speeds it up. A person who drinks a cup containing 100 milligrams of caffeine at 3 p.m. may therefore still have about 50 milligrams in the body at 8 p.m. and about 25 milligrams at 1 a.m.

(4) That lingering caffeine can matter even for people who fall asleep easily. In one laboratory study, adults who took a large dose of caffeine six hours before bedtime slept about an hour less, on average, than when they took a placebo, yet many of them did not notice the difference. Short sleep, in turn, can leave a person tired the next morning and reaching for more coffee, a cycle that is easy to fall into.

(5) None of this means caffeine is harmful for most people. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration considers up to 400 milligrams a day, about four or five cups of brewed coffee, an amount not generally linked to harmful effects in healthy adults. For a good night's sleep, the timing of the last cup may matter as much as the total.

RC05.t: Keeping Food Out of the Danger Zone
RC05.p:
(1) The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about 48 million people in the United States get sick from foodborne illness each year. Not every case begins in a restaurant. In home kitchens, familiar habits, such as leaving a pot of chili on the stove to cool overnight or thawing a roast on the counter, give bacteria exactly what they need to grow: moisture, food and warmth.

(2) Food safety experts call the range between 40°F and 140°F the "danger zone." Within it, many bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes. Food held in this range too long may look and smell normal while carrying enough bacteria to make someone sick. For that reason, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) advises refrigerating perishable food within two hours of cooking, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 90°F, as it often is at a summer picnic.

(3) Cooling food quickly matters as much as cooling it at all. A large pot of soup placed in the refrigerator whole may stay warm in its center for hours, because heat escapes slowly from a deep container. Dividing leftovers into shallow containers lets them chill quickly and evenly. The refrigerator itself should be set at 40°F or below, and the freezer at 0°F.

(4) Thawing is another weak point. The outside of a frozen roast left on the counter can warm into the danger zone while its center is still icy. The USDA recommends three safe methods instead: thawing in the refrigerator, in cold water that is changed every 30 minutes, or in the microwave. Food thawed in cold water or in the microwave should be cooked right away. The refrigerator method is the slowest, needing about a day for every 4 to 5 pounds of food, but the food stays cold the whole time. Planning a meal a day ahead is a small price to pay for that peace of mind.

(5) Finally, a food thermometer settles questions that color and texture cannot. Poultry is safe to eat once it reaches an internal temperature of 165°F, and ground beef once it reaches 160°F. Leftovers should be reheated to 165°F. Together, prompt cooling, safe thawing and thorough cooking keep bacteria from multiplying to harmful numbers.

RC06.t: Every Adult Should Know Hands-Only CPR
RC06.p:
(1) Each year, more than 350,000 people in the United States have a cardiac arrest outside a hospital, and most of them do not survive. In cardiac arrest, the heart suddenly stops pumping blood effectively, and without help a person can die within minutes. Yet in many of these emergencies, the people standing closest do not step in, not because they do not care but because they do not know what to do. That has to change.

(2) The good news is that the skill they need is simpler than most people think. The American Heart Association recommends hands-only CPR for anyone who sees a teen or adult suddenly collapse. It has just two steps: call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute, until help arrives. No rescue breaths are needed. The compressions keep oxygen-rich blood moving to the brain until paramedics or a defibrillator can restore a normal heart rhythm. Prompt bystander CPR can double or even triple a person's chance of survival.

(3) Some people hold back because they are afraid of hurting the victim or of being sued. These worries are understandable, but they are misplaced. Every state has a Good Samaritan law that offers legal protection to people who give reasonable help in an emergency. And without CPR, a person in cardiac arrest is very unlikely to survive, so the risk of acting is far smaller than the risk of standing by.

(4) Learning takes less time than a lunch break. Free online videos teach the basic technique in a few minutes, and many fire departments and hospitals offer short hands-on sessions. Many states now require high school students to learn CPR before they graduate. Every state should adopt that rule. Employers, too, should offer training to every worker.

(5) No one can predict where a cardiac arrest will happen: at a ballgame, in an office, or at the kitchen table. But each of us can decide today to be ready. Watch a video, sign up for a class, and practice the rhythm. The next life saved could belong to someone you love.

RC07.p:
(1) On her third night as a certified nursing assistant, Lena Ortiz was already behind. Call lights blinked down the hallway of the medical unit, and the charge nurse had reminded her twice to finish recording vital signs before midnight. So when Mr. Halvorsen in Room 412 pushed away his dinner tray for the second evening in a row, Lena felt a flash of frustration. She noted "refused meal" in his record and hurried on.

(2) An hour later, she passed his room again. The television was off, and the eighty-one-year-old retired machinist sat upright in bed, staring at the dark window. Something about the stillness made Lena stop. She asked whether he needed anything. He shook his head, then said, almost to himself, "My wife always cut the meat for me. My hands don't work like they used to."

(3) Lena looked at his hands, swollen at the knuckles and curled stiffly around the edge of the blanket. She had seen the tray as something he had chosen not to eat, not as something he could not manage. She reported his words to the nurse, who arranged for the kitchen to send softer food already cut into small pieces and asked an occupational therapist to bring utensils with thick, padded handles.

(4) The next evening, Mr. Halvorsen finished nearly everything on his plate. While Lena collected the tray, he told her about the forty years he had spent repairing tractors, and about his wife, Ruth, who had died the previous spring. Lena stayed only five minutes, but she left the room feeling that it was the most useful thing she had done all week.

(5) Years later, as a registered nurse who trains new assistants, Lena still tells them about Room 412. Records, she reminds them, show what patients do; they rarely explain why. Sometimes the only way to learn the reason is to slow down long enough to ask.

RC08.t: The Salt We Do Not See
RC08.p:
(1) Most Americans think of salt as something they add from a shaker, but the shaker is a small part of the story. Salt is made of sodium and chloride, and it is the sodium that matters most for health. Federal dietary guidelines advise adults to keep sodium below 2,300 milligrams a day, about the amount in one teaspoon of table salt. The average American adult eats about 3,400 milligrams a day, nearly 50 percent more than that limit.

(2) Where does the extra sodium come from? Studies of American diets find that more than 70 percent of the sodium people eat is already in food before it reaches the table: it is added during processing or by restaurant cooks. Bread, deli meats, pizza, canned soups and packaged snacks are among the largest sources. Many of these foods do not taste especially salty, which is one reason people underestimate how much sodium they eat. A single slice of bread may hold 100 to 200 milligrams, but bread eaten several times a day adds up quickly.

(3) Sodium matters because of its effect on blood pressure. When a person eats more sodium than the body needs, the kidneys hold on to extra water to dilute it. The added fluid raises the volume of blood moving through the vessels, and the higher volume pushes harder against the vessel walls. Over years, high blood pressure strains the heart and blood vessels and raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Not everyone's blood pressure responds to sodium to the same degree, but in large studies, people who cut back on sodium tend to see their blood pressure fall.

(4) Because so much sodium is hidden, shoppers need a way to find it. Reading the Nutrition Facts label is one of the most practical tools a shopper has. The label lists sodium in milligrams per serving and as a percent Daily Value. As a rough guide, 5 percent Daily Value or less per serving is considered low, and 20 percent or more is considered high. Shoppers should also check the serving size: a can of soup that lists 700 milligrams per serving may hold two servings.

(5) Some cities and food companies have begun working to lower sodium across the food supply, since individual effort can go only so far when most sodium is added before purchase. Until those efforts reach every grocery aisle, the most reliable approach is to cook more meals at home, choose fresh foods over processed ones when possible, and compare labels before buying.

RC09.p:
(1) Antibiotics are among the most useful medicines ever developed. Infections that once killed many people, such as pneumonia and infected wounds, can usually be cured with a short course of pills. But every use of an antibiotic carries a hidden cost: it gives bacteria a chance to adapt. When bacteria can survive the drugs designed to kill them, they are called antibiotic-resistant, and the infections they cause become harder, and sometimes impossible, to treat.

(2) Resistance develops through a kind of natural selection. In any large group of bacteria, a few may carry a genetic change that lets them survive a particular drug. When an antibiotic kills the others, those few are left with less competition, and they multiply. Over time, the resistant type can become the most common one. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes to one another, so a trait that appears in one kind of bacteria can spread to others.

(3) The scale of the problem is large. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that more than 2.8 million antibiotic-resistant infections occur in the United States each year and that more than 35,000 people die as a result. Because resistant infections often require longer hospital stays and more expensive drugs, they also add billions of dollars to health care costs.

(4) Much of the pressure comes from antibiotics that were not needed in the first place. Antibiotics work against bacteria, but most colds, most sore throats and the flu are caused by viruses, which antibiotics cannot kill. The CDC estimates that at least 28 percent of the antibiotics prescribed in doctors' offices and clinics are unnecessary. Each unneeded prescription exposes the bacteria a person normally carries to the drug without any benefit to the patient.

(5) Patients can help slow resistance. They can avoid pressing for an antibiotic when a provider says an illness is viral, take any antibiotic exactly as prescribed, and never share leftover pills or save them for later. Hand washing and staying up to date on recommended vaccines also help, because every infection that is prevented is one that does not need treatment. Antibiotics will stay useful as long as they are used with care.

RC10.t: Why the Body Runs a Fever
RC10.p:
(1) A fever can feel like a sign that the body's machinery has broken down, but in most cases it shows that the body's defenses are working. A fever is a body temperature above the normal range, which for most adults centers around 98.6°F (37°C), although normal temperature varies from person to person and through the day. Many doctors consider 100.4°F (38°C) or higher to be a fever.

(2) Body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain that works much like a thermostat. When the immune system detects an infection, white blood cells release chemical messengers, some of which travel to the hypothalamus and raise its set point. The brain now treats the body as too cold for the new target. In response, blood vessels in the skin narrow to hold in heat, and muscles begin to shiver to produce more. This is why a person with a rising fever often feels chilled and reaches for a blanket even while the skin feels warm to someone else.

(3) Why would the body heat itself on purpose? A higher temperature appears to help the immune system in several ways. Many bacteria and viruses multiply best at normal body temperature, so a few degrees of extra heat can slow their growth. Some white blood cells also move and work faster when the body is warmer.

(4) Eventually, as the infection is brought under control, the chemical messengers fade and the set point returns to normal. Now the body is warmer than its target, so it works to shed heat: the skin flushes as its blood vessels widen, and the person begins to sweat. People often say a fever has "broken" when this sweating begins.

(5) A fever is not harmless in every case. Very high temperatures can be dangerous, and young infants, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may need prompt care even for a moderate fever. Medicines that lower fever can make a person more comfortable, and many doctors recommend them for that reason. For a healthy adult with a mild fever, though, the rise in temperature is usually less a problem to be fixed than a clue that the body is fighting back.

RC11.t: From Lab to Clinic: How Vaccines Are Tested
RC11.p:
(1) Before a new vaccine can be offered to the public in the United States, it must pass through a long series of tests. The process is designed to answer two questions: Is the vaccine safe, and does it work? Each stage builds on the one before it, and a vaccine that raises serious concerns at any stage can be stopped.

(2) Testing begins in the laboratory and in animals. If these early studies are promising, the developer asks the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for permission to begin testing in people. Human testing, called clinical trials, usually takes place in three phases. In Phase 1, a small group of healthy adults, often 20 to 100 volunteers, receives the vaccine. Researchers look mainly for side effects and try to find a safe dose.

(3) Phase 2 expands the study to several hundred people, often including people similar to those the vaccine is meant to protect, such as older adults or children. Researchers continue to watch for side effects and begin to measure how the immune system responds. Phase 3 is the largest stage, enrolling thousands or even tens of thousands of volunteers. Usually, some volunteers receive the vaccine and others receive a placebo, a look-alike shot with no active ingredient. Neither the volunteers nor the researchers giving the shots know who received which, so their expectations cannot sway the results. By comparing how many people in each group become ill, researchers can judge how well the vaccine prevents disease.

(4) When Phase 3 is complete, the developer submits all of its data to the FDA. Agency scientists review the results, inspect the factory where the vaccine will be made, and often consult a panel of outside experts before deciding whether to license the vaccine. Even after approval, monitoring continues. Systems such as the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) collect reports of health problems after vaccination, allowing rare side effects that did not appear in trials to be detected.

(5) Critics sometimes say this process takes too long, and it has often taken ten years or more. Supporters reply that the length of the process is the reason the public can trust its results. In emergencies, some steps can overlap or be sped up, but the basic phases are kept.

RC12.p:
(1) Walk through almost any park or school in America and you will find drinking fountains that are broken, taped over or simply gone. Many were shut off during the COVID-19 pandemic and have stayed off since. That is a mistake our communities can no longer afford. Every public park and school should have a working water station. City councils should pay for them now.

(2) The case begins with health. Children who drink water instead of sugary drinks take in fewer empty calories, and water has no sugar to feed tooth decay. When water is free and easy to reach, people drink more of it. One study found that middle school students drank more water after new filling stations were installed. When water is hard to find, the vending machine down the hall becomes the easy choice.

(3) Money is the second reason. A family that buys a case of bottled water every week can spend hundreds of dollars a year on something that flows from the tap for pennies. A modern station with a bottle filler costs a few thousand dollars to install, far less than many of the playground upgrades councils approve without debate. Many stations even display a counter showing how many plastic bottles they have replaced.

(4) Some council members worry about cleanliness, and that concern deserves a real answer. Today's stations are not the rusty fountains of the past. Bottle fillers let people refill without putting their mouths near the spout, and many include filters that are changed on a schedule. A station that is cleaned and checked like any other public equipment is as safe as the tap in your own kitchen.

(5) Finally, there is the question of fairness. Families with money can carry bottled water or buy a drink at the snack bar. Children whose families cannot afford bottled water should not have to choose between thirst and soda. A drinking fountain is one of the few places in a city where anyone, rich or poor, is welcome to take what they need.

(6) Our council will vote on next year's parks budget in March. I urge every reader to attend the meeting, or to write to a council member, and ask for one simple line item: working water in every park and school.

RC13.p:
(1) When my father was told he had type 2 diabetes, he came home from the clinic, set the pamphlets on the kitchen table and went out to mow a lawn that did not need mowing. He was sixty-one, a retired bus mechanic who had never spent a night in a hospital, and he did not intend to start thinking of himself as a patient.

(2) The nurse had shown him how to use a glucose meter, a small device that measures the sugar in a drop of blood. For the first two weeks, the meter stayed in its zippered case beside the toaster. When I asked about it, he said he felt fine, and feeling fine, in his view, was all the information a man needed. I was nineteen and in my first semester of nursing prerequisites, and I knew enough to worry but not enough to know what to say.

(3) So I tried an approach I hoped he would respect. I drew a grid on a sheet of poster board, with the days of the week across the top and "Before breakfast" and "Two hours after dinner" down the side, and I taped it to the refrigerator. I didn't lecture. I simply checked my own blood pressure each morning with the cuff from my anatomy kit and recorded the numbers in a corner of the chart, where he could see them.

(4) For four days he walked past it. On the fifth morning, I came downstairs to find the meter case open on the counter and a number written in pencil in the first empty box, in my father's square, careful handwriting. He didn't mention it, and neither did I.

(5) By the end of the month, the chart was full, and he had started a second one himself, adding a column for what he ate. He began to talk about his numbers the way he used to talk about engines: what made them run rough, what made them run smooth. At his three-month visit, the nurse told him his results had improved, and he came home and told me as if he had rebuilt a transmission.

(6) I have since learned many better ways to teach patients, but I still think about that sheet of poster board. My father did not need more facts. He needed a way to take charge that felt like his own idea.

RC14.t: First Aid for a Minor Burn
RC14.p:
(1) Most burns that happen at home, such as a splash from a pot of boiling pasta or a quick touch of a hot pan, are minor. A minor burn affects the outer layer of skin, or the outer layer and part of the layer beneath it, and covers a small area. It may turn red, swell and form small blisters. With the right first aid, most minor burns heal in one to three weeks. The wrong first aid, however, can deepen the injury or invite infection.

(2) Step 1: Cool the burn. Hold the burned area under cool, not cold, running water for about 10 minutes, or until the pain eases. If running water is not available, use a clean cloth soaked in cool water. Do not use ice or ice water. Extreme cold narrows the blood vessels in the skin and can damage tissue that is already injured.

(3) Step 2: Remove tight items. While cooling the burn, gently take off rings, watches, bracelets or snug clothing near the burned area. Burned skin swells quickly, and an item that slides off easily now may have to be cut off an hour later.

(4) Step 3: Protect the skin. Leave small blisters alone. A blister's roof is a natural barrier that keeps germs away from the raw skin underneath; if a blister breaks on its own, wash the area gently with mild soap and water. Cover the burn loosely with a sterile nonstick bandage or clean gauze, since wrapping it tightly puts pressure on the swollen skin. Skip home remedies such as butter, oil or toothpaste, which hold in heat and may carry bacteria.

(5) Step 4: Manage pain and watch for trouble. An over-the-counter pain reliever, taken as the label directs, can ease discomfort. Over the next several days, watch for signs of infection, such as increasing pain, redness that spreads, swelling, oozing or fever. Get medical care for any of these signs, and seek care right away for any burn that is larger than about 3 inches across, that is on the face, hands, feet, groin or a major joint, or that looks white, leathery or charred.

RC15.t: The Score in the First Minute
RC15.p:
(1) Before the 1950s, a newborn who looked healthy at a glance was often given little further attention in the delivery room. Doctors and nurses focused on the mother, and a baby who was struggling to breathe could go unnoticed for several critical minutes. There was no shared, quick method for judging how well a newborn was adjusting to life outside the womb.

(2) Dr. Virginia Apgar, an anesthesiologist at a hospital in New York City, set out to change that. Having watched many births from her place beside the operating table, she noticed that staff described newborns in vague terms such as "fine" or "a little weak." In 1952 she proposed a simple scoring system, and she published it the following year. Her method asked the person attending the birth to check five signs: heart rate, breathing effort, muscle tone, reflex response, and skin color. Each sign received a score of 0, 1, or 2, so a baby's total could range from 0 to 10.

(3) The appeal of the system lay in its speed. The score could be assigned in less than a minute without any special equipment, and it gave everyone in the room a common language. Instead of debating whether a baby looked weak, staff could report a number. Apgar recommended taking the score one minute after birth. The practice of repeating it at five minutes became standard later, because the second score showed whether a baby was improving.

(4) The score was not designed to predict a child's long-term health or intelligence, and medical groups today caution against using it that way. Its purpose was narrower: to signal, in the first moments of life, which babies needed help right away. Even so, the score had an effect beyond the delivery room. Because it turned a newborn's condition into a number that could be recorded and compared, researchers could study which practices during labor were linked to healthier babies.

(5) Today the Apgar score is used in hospitals around the world, and nearly every baby born in a hospital in the United States receives one. Many parents hear the numbers within minutes of the birth, often without knowing that they come from the careful observations of one physician who believed that every newborn deserved a closer look.

RC16.p:
(1) Hospitals are built to help people heal, yet many patients say they sleep worse there than anywhere else. Alarms beep, carts rattle down hallways, and staff members talk outside doors at all hours. Poor sleep is more than an annoyance: patients who sleep badly often report more pain and lower mood, and they may recover more slowly.

(2) In 2023, the staff of a 32-bed medical unit at one regional hospital decided to measure the problem. For two weeks, sound meters placed in the hallway recorded noise levels between 11 p.m. and 5 a.m. The average was 58 decibels, about the level of a normal conversation, and peaks above 80 decibels occurred several times each night. On a morning survey, 61 percent of patients rated their sleep as "poor" or "very poor."

(3) The unit then introduced "quiet hours" from 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. Hallway lights were dimmed, staff moved conversations away from patient rooms, and nonurgent tasks such as restocking supplies were moved to the evening. Patients were offered earplugs and eye masks. Routine vital signs for stable patients were scheduled so that a patient was not awakened more than once during quiet hours unless the patient's condition required it.

(4) After three months, the same meters showed an average nighttime level of 49 decibels, and peaks above 80 decibels had become rare. The share of patients rating their sleep as poor or very poor fell to 37 percent. Requests for sleep medication also dropped, from an average of 9 per night to 6.

(5) The unit's nurse manager called the program "the most worthwhile change our staff has made in years." The team is careful, however, about what the numbers show. The survey was not designed as a controlled experiment, and the patients surveyed after the change were different people, with different illnesses, from those surveyed before. The unit also opened a new family lounge during the same months, which moved some visitor conversations off the hallway. The team plans to repeat the measurements next year on two other units.

RC17.p:
(1) High blood pressure often causes no symptoms, yet over time it strains the heart and blood vessels and raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Regular physical activity is one of the changes health professionals most often recommend, along with eating less salt and taking medication when it is prescribed. For many adults, the hard part is not knowing what to do but finding a way to keep doing it.

(2) In the spring of 2024, a community health center in a mid-sized city invited adults with high blood pressure to join a free 12-week walking program. Participants met in groups of 10 to 12 at a city park three mornings a week. Each group was led by a trained volunteer, and walks began at 20 minutes and grew to 45 minutes by the sixth week. A nurse measured each participant's blood pressure at the start and at the end of the program.

(3) Of the 240 adults who enrolled, 172 completed all 12 weeks. Among those who finished, average systolic blood pressure, the top number in a reading, fell by 6 points. The 68 participants who left early were not measured again, so their results are unknown. Of those who could be reached by phone, most said that their work schedules had changed or that they had moved away.

(4) Group members described the walks as social events as much as exercise. Several said they came on rainy mornings mainly because they did not want to let their group down. The volunteer leaders noticed a related pattern: attendance was highest in groups whose members began arranging rides for one another and lowest in groups that changed leaders partway through.

(5) The health center plans to offer the program again next spring. This time, staff will also track a comparison group of adults who are on the waiting list, and they will contact everyone who leaves early to measure their blood pressure one last time.

RC18.p:
(1) When a food disagrees with someone, people often say they are "allergic" to it. In medical terms, however, a food allergy and a food intolerance are different problems. They can cause some of the same discomfort, but they begin in different parts of the body and carry very different levels of risk.

(2) A food allergy begins in the immune system, the body's defense against germs. In a person with an allergy, the immune system mistakes a protein in a food, such as peanuts, eggs, or shellfish, for a threat. The next time the person eats that food, the body releases chemicals that can cause hives, swelling of the lips or throat, vomiting, or trouble breathing. Even a trace amount of the food can set off a reaction. In the most serious cases, a reaction called anaphylaxis affects several body systems at once and can become life-threatening within minutes.

(3) A food intolerance, by contrast, usually begins in the digestive system. Lactose intolerance is a common example. People with this condition make too little lactase, the enzyme that breaks down the sugar in milk. When undigested lactose reaches the large intestine, it can cause gas, bloating, cramps, or diarrhea. These symptoms can be unpleasant, but they are not life-threatening, and they often depend on the amount eaten. Many people with lactose intolerance can drink a small glass of milk or eat a little cheese without trouble.

(4) Because the two conditions are managed differently, the distinction matters. A person with a food allergy is usually told to avoid the food completely, to read ingredient labels with care, and, in some cases, to carry an epinephrine auto-injector for emergencies. A person with an intolerance may need only to limit portions or to choose products made for easier digestion, such as lactose-free milk.

(5) Symptoms do not always reveal which problem a person has, since vomiting or stomach pain can occur with either. For that reason, anyone who suspects a food allergy should talk with a health care provider, who can order tests and recommend a plan. Guessing could lead a person to avoid foods that are safe to eat or, more seriously, to take chances with a food that could cause a dangerous reaction.

RC19.p:
(1) A vaccine can be produced with great care and still fail to protect the person who receives it if it has been stored at the wrong temperature along the way. Many vaccines lose strength when they become too warm, and some are damaged by freezing. The system of refrigerators, freezers, insulated containers, and temperature records that keeps vaccines within a safe range from the factory to the clinic is known as the "cold chain."

(2) Most routine vaccines given in doctors' offices are kept refrigerated between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, or roughly 36 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit. A few must be stored frozen. Each step in the journey, from the manufacturer's warehouse to a delivery truck to the clinic's storage unit, is a link in the chain, and a problem at any link can affect every dose that passes through it.

(3) Damage is not always easy to see. A vaccine that has been overheated or frozen often looks exactly like one that has been stored properly. For this reason, clinics rely on records rather than appearance. Many use digital data loggers, small devices that record the temperature inside a storage unit at regular intervals and sound an alarm if it drifts out of the safe range. Staff review the readings at least once each workday.

(4) When a storage unit has been out of range, the clinic does not simply throw the vaccines away or go on using them. Staff label the affected doses "Do not use," keep them in proper storage, and contact the manufacturer or the health department, which decides whether the doses can still be given.

(5) Household refrigerators, especially small dormitory-style units, are poorly suited to vaccine storage. Their temperatures can swing widely, and the area near the cooling vent can freeze vaccines placed too close to it. Every clinic that gives vaccines should invest in a storage unit built for the purpose; the cost is modest next to the cost of wasted doses and lost public trust.

RC20.p:
(1) More than 100,000 people in the United States are on the national waiting list for an organ transplant, and about 17 of them die each day before an organ becomes available. Most are waiting for a kidney; others need a liver, a heart or a lung. Seventeen deaths a day is a toll no caring society should accept. Part of the reason for the shortage is simple: not enough people have said yes to donation, and that is something every adult can help change.

(2) Signing up is easy. In most states, adults can register when they apply for or renew a driver's license, or at any time through a state or national online registry, at no cost. Registration matters more than many people realize, because very few deaths make donation possible. Only about 3 in every 1,000 people die in a way that allows their organs to be used. When donation is possible, a single donor can save as many as eight lives.

(3) Some people hold back because they fear that doctors will not try as hard to save a registered donor, or because they believe their religion forbids donation. These fears are understandable, and they deserve a careful answer. The doctors who treat an injured patient are separate from the transplant team, and donation is considered only after every effort to save the patient has failed and death has been declared. Most major religions in the United States support donation. Others assume they are too old or too sick to qualify, but there is no upper age limit for registering, and doctors decide at the time of death which organs can be used.

(4) Registering also spares families a painful choice. When someone dies without having made their wishes known, relatives must decide about donation on one of the hardest days of their lives. Many say no simply because they are unsure what their loved one would have wanted. A name on the registry answers that question in advance, and a conversation at the kitchen table makes the answer clearer still.

(5) If you have not yet registered, take a few minutes this week to do it, and then tell the people closest to you. Few decisions ask so little of us and offer so much to strangers. One checked box could someday give another family years with someone they love.

RC21.t: Using an Inhaler with a Spacer
RC21.p:
(1) A metered-dose inhaler delivers medicine straight to the lungs, but only if the medicine gets there. When the inhaler is used by itself, much of each puff can land on the tongue and the back of the throat instead. A spacer, a tube that attaches to the mouthpiece of the inhaler, holds the puff of medicine for a moment so that you can breathe it in slowly. Your health care provider or pharmacist can show you which spacer fits your inhaler. The steps below describe how to use one.

(2) Before you begin, remove the caps from the inhaler and the spacer and check that nothing is inside the spacer. Shake the inhaler well for about five seconds, then fit its mouthpiece into the opening at the end of the spacer. If your inhaler is new or has not been used for a while, follow the package directions for priming it, which usually means spraying it into the air a few times first.

(3) Stand or sit up straight and breathe out fully, away from the spacer. Then place the spacer's mouthpiece between your teeth and close your lips around it to form a seal. Press the inhaler once to release one puff into the spacer. Breathe in slowly and deeply through your mouth. If your spacer whistles, you are breathing in too fast. Remove the spacer from your mouth and hold your breath for up to 10 seconds, or as long as is comfortable, before breathing out slowly.

(4) If your provider has prescribed a second puff, wait about 30 seconds to one minute, shake the inhaler again, and repeat the steps. Do not place two puffs in the spacer at the same time. If your inhaler contains a steroid medicine, rinse your mouth with water and spit it out after your last puff; this helps prevent a mouth infection called thrush.

(5) Clean the spacer about once a week, or as the package directs. Many spacers should be washed in warm water with a little dish soap and left to air-dry rather than rubbed with a towel, because towel drying can create static that makes the medicine cling to the inside walls. Paying attention to these small details helps each puff of medicine work as well as it should.

RC22.p:
(1) The human body works best within a narrow temperature range, close to 98.6°F (37°C). When the body heats up during exercise or on a hot day, the brain responds by widening blood vessels near the skin and switching on the sweat glands. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the skin. This cooling system is remarkably effective, but it has limits, and when those limits are reached, heat-related illness can follow.

(2) Several conditions make the system less efficient. In humid air, sweat evaporates slowly, so much of it drips off the skin instead of cooling it. A person who has not been drinking enough fluid may produce less sweat. Heavy clothing traps warm air against the body, and strenuous work generates far more heat than resting does. These factors often occur together, as when a roofer works through a muggy July afternoon.

(3) Heat exhaustion is the milder of the two main heat illnesses. A person with heat exhaustion usually sweats heavily and may feel weak, dizzy or nauseated. The skin is often cool and clammy, and the pulse may be fast and weak. Moving to a cooler place, loosening clothing and sipping water usually bring improvement within an hour.

(4) Heat stroke, by contrast, is a medical emergency. Body temperature climbs to 103°F (39.4°C) or higher as the body's cooling system begins to fail. The skin may be hot and red, and it can be either dry or damp. Unlike the person with heat exhaustion, who generally remains alert, someone with heat stroke may become confused, slur words or lose consciousness. Without rapid cooling, heat stroke can damage the brain and other organs. Heat exhaustion that is not treated can progress to heat stroke.

(5) Some groups face greater risk. Older adults may not sense thirst as sharply as younger people, and infants depend on others to keep them cool. Outdoor workers and athletes who train in summer are exposed for long periods. Health officials advise these groups to drink water regularly, schedule hard activity for cooler hours and take breaks in the shade. Recognizing the early signs of heat exhaustion gives people a chance to act before a dangerous condition develops.

RC23.p:
(1) Missed medical appointments are more than an inconvenience. When a patient does not show up, the time slot usually goes unused, other patients wait longer for care, and the person who missed the visit may go without a needed checkup or prescription refill. At Eastside Family Clinic, about 18 percent of scheduled visits in 2023 were missed without notice, a rate staff described as "a hole in every afternoon."

(2) In January 2024, the clinic began sending each patient a text message two days before a visit, with a link to confirm or cancel. Over the next six months, the no-show rate fell to 11 percent. Patients also used the link to cancel about 300 visits ahead of time, and staff filled most of those openings with patients from a waiting list.

(3) Before crediting the texts, clinic leaders looked more closely. Westside Family Clinic, run by the same organization and serving similar patients, did not send texts during those months. Its no-show rate also dropped, from 17 percent to 15 percent, perhaps because both clinics added evening hours in January. Comparing the two suggests that something other than the texts accounted for part of Eastside's improvement, but that the texts likely made a difference beyond it.

(4) The reminders did not work equally well for everyone. Patients aged 65 and older, many of whom said in a survey that they rarely read text messages, missed visits at nearly the same rate as before. For that group, the clinic is now testing automated phone calls.

(5) The clinic's director calls the program "the best money we have ever spent," noting that the texting service costs about $400 a month. Other staff members are more measured. They point out that six months is a short period and that the results come from one clinic. Westside plans to begin sending texts in July, which will show whether its patients respond the same way.

RC24.p:
(1) In the early 1900s, doctors in parts of the United States noticed a striking pattern. Around the Great Lakes, in the Appalachian Mountains and across the Pacific Northwest, large numbers of people had a goiter, a visible swelling at the front of the neck caused by an enlarged thyroid gland. The area became known as the "goiter belt." During World War I, goiter was a common reason that young men from these regions were turned away from military service.

(2) The thyroid uses iodine to make hormones that help control how the body uses energy. When the diet supplies too little iodine, the gland enlarges as it works harder to make enough hormone. People get iodine mainly from food and water, and the amount in local crops depends on the soil. In the goiter belt, the soil was low in iodine, so people who ate mostly local food took in too little.

(3) Researchers in Ohio tested a simple remedy in the late 1910s. Schoolgirls in Akron who took small doses of iodine developed goiter far less often than classmates who did not. Health officials then looked for a way to deliver iodine to everyone without asking people to change their habits. Salt was an ideal carrier: nearly everyone used it, in fairly steady amounts, every day. In 1924, iodized salt went on sale in Michigan, and a national salt company soon offered it across the country.

(4) The change worked quickly. Within a few years, surveys of Michigan schoolchildren found far fewer cases of goiter than before, and the goiter belt gradually faded as a medical concern. Today, a quarter teaspoon of iodized salt supplies roughly half of the iodine an adult needs each day, which is about 150 micrograms.

(5) Iodized salt remains a choice rather than a requirement in the United States. Most of the salt in packaged and restaurant foods is not iodized, and many specialty salts, such as sea salt and kosher salt, usually contain little or no added iodine. People who cook with these salts and eat few dairy products, eggs or seafood, which are other good sources, may get less iodine than they need. Pregnant women need more than other adults, about 220 micrograms a day, because the developing baby depends on it.

RC25.p:
(1) Lead was once a common ingredient in house paint because it made paint more durable and helped it dry quickly. The United States banned lead-based paint for homes in 1978, but millions of houses and apartments built before then still contain it, often hidden under newer layers. As long as the old paint stays intact, it poses little danger. The trouble begins when it chips, peels or is disturbed.

(2) Young children face the greatest risk. When old paint wears down, especially on surfaces that rub together, such as window frames and doors, it releases fine dust that settles on floors and windowsills. Children under 6 crawl, play on the floor and put their hands and toys in their mouths, so they swallow far more of this dust than adults do. Their growing bodies also absorb more of the lead they take in.

(3) Lead harms the developing brain and nervous system. Even low levels in the blood have been linked to learning problems, shorter attention spans and lower scores on tests of thinking skills, and health agencies say that no safe blood lead level in children has been identified. Much of this damage cannot be undone. Yet most children with raised lead levels look and act healthy, so a blood test is the one reliable way to know whether a child has been exposed.

(4) Families can lower the risk in several ways. Wet-mopping floors and wiping windowsills with a damp cloth removes dust without stirring it into the air, while dry sweeping can spread it. Washing children's hands and toys often, especially before meals and naps, reduces how much dust reaches their mouths. Peeling paint should be covered or repaired by someone trained in lead-safe methods rather than scraped.

(5) Renovation deserves particular care. Sanding, scraping or tearing out painted surfaces in an older home can fill a room with lead dust in minutes. Federal rules require contractors who work on homes built before 1978 to be certified in lead-safe practices, and parents planning a project should ask to see that certification. Families with young children in older homes should also ask the child's health care provider about lead testing.

RC26.p:
(1) Last spring, a second grader at Lincoln Elementary began wheezing during recess. The school secretary, who had received a few hours of first aid training, found the boy's inhaler, called his mother and waited. The boy recovered, and the secretary deserves our thanks. But she should not have been the most qualified health worker in the building.

(2) In our district, three of eleven schools have a registered nurse on site every school day. The other eight share two nurses who travel between buildings, which means a nurse may be twenty minutes or more away when a child needs one. Meanwhile, the number of students who come to school with a long-term health condition keeps growing. This year, district records list 214 students with asthma, 38 with type 1 diabetes and 96 with an allergy severe enough to require an epinephrine injector.

(3) A school nurse does far more than hand out bandages. The nurse checks a diabetic student's blood sugar before lunch, trains teachers to recognize an allergic reaction, notices the child who visits the office every Monday with a stomachache, and follows up with families when a vision screening suggests a problem. Students whose health needs are managed at school spend more time in class, and time in class is the whole point of a school.

(4) Some board members argue that the district cannot afford eight more full-time nurses, and the cost is real: roughly $70,000 a year for each position, including benefits. Yet the district already pays for substitutes when teachers leave class to handle medical problems, and it pays in lost learning every time a student is sent home for a problem a nurse could have managed. A phased plan, adding three nurses next year and the rest over the following two years, would spread the cost.

(5) The board will vote on next year's budget in May. I urge every parent who has ever worried about a child's health at school to attend that meeting or write to the board before then. Our children deserve a nurse down the hall, not across town.

RC27.p:
(1) On a July evening in 1893, a young man named James Cornish was carried into a small Chicago hospital with a stab wound to the chest. At the time, surgeons rarely operated inside the chest, because bleeding and infection made such operations deadly. X-rays had not yet been discovered, and safe blood transfusions and antibiotics were still decades away. The surgeon on duty, Daniel Hale Williams, chose with remarkable courage to operate anyway. He opened the chest, repaired a tear in the sac surrounding the heart and closed the wound. Cornish left the hospital several weeks later and lived for many years.

(2) Williams's road to that operating room had been anything but smooth. Born in Hollidaysburg, Pennsylvania, in 1856, he lost his father when he was a boy and was sent to work as a shoemaker's apprentice. He later moved to Wisconsin, where he cut hair in a barbershop, studied in his spare hours and then trained under a local physician. In 1883 he graduated from Chicago Medical College.

(3) As a young doctor in Chicago, Williams saw that Black patients were often refused care or treated poorly at hospitals, and that Black women who hoped to become nurses were shut out of training schools. In 1891 he answered both problems at once by founding Provident Hospital, which accepted patients of every race and ran a nursing school open to Black women. It was at Provident that he operated on Cornish two years later.

(4) Williams devoted much of his later career to building institutions. In 1894 he became chief surgeon at Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, D.C., where he reorganized the staff and started a training program for nurses. In 1895 he helped found the National Medical Association, a professional society for Black physicians, who were largely excluded from the American Medical Association. In 1913 he became the first Black member of the newly formed American College of Surgeons.

(5) Williams died in 1931. The 1893 operation made his name, but his most lasting gift may be the hospitals, training programs and professional groups he built with such tireless energy. They went on caring for patients and preparing nurses and doctors for generations after his own operating days had ended.

RC28.t: Checking Your Blood Pressure at Home
RC28.p:
(1) Your health care provider has asked you to check your blood pressure at home. Home readings show how your pressure behaves during ordinary life, away from the stress some people feel in a clinic. To be useful, though, every reading must be taken the same careful way. Follow the steps below, and bring your record to each appointment. In our view, few habits give you and your provider more useful information for less effort.

(2) Before you measure: Choose times you can repeat every day, such as before breakfast and again in the evening. For at least 30 minutes beforehand, do not exercise, smoke, or drink coffee, tea or other drinks with caffeine. Empty your bladder, because a full bladder can raise your reading. Then sit quietly in a chair with your back supported for five minutes, without talking or looking at your phone.

(3) Position yourself and the cuff: Keep both feet flat on the floor and your legs uncrossed. Rest your arm on a table so that the middle of your upper arm is level with your heart. Wrap the cuff around bare skin, not over a sleeve, with its lower edge about one inch above the bend of your elbow. The cuff should be snug, but you should be able to slip two fingertips under its top edge.

(4) Take and record the readings: Press the start button and stay still and silent while the cuff inflates and releases. When the numbers appear, write down both of them, the top (systolic) and bottom (diastolic), along with the date and time. Wait one minute, then take a second reading and record it as well. Keep a written log even if your monitor stores results, since some models erase stored readings when the batteries are changed.

(5) Know when to call: One high reading is not usually a cause for alarm, because pressure rises and falls throughout the day. If your readings stay above the goal your provider gave you for several days, call the office. If your top number is higher than 180 or your bottom number is higher than 120, wait five minutes and measure again. If it is still that high, call your provider right away; if you also have chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, a change in vision or trouble speaking, call 911.

RC29.p:
(1) Most people have stepped out of a loud concert or a noisy workshop and noticed a faint ringing that was not there before. For many, the sound fades within a day. For others, it lingers for months or never fully leaves. This experience of hearing a sound that has no outside source is called tinnitus. It may ring, hiss, buzz, roar or whistle, and it may be heard in one ear or both.

(2) Tinnitus is not a disease in itself but a symptom. The most common trigger is damage to the inner ear. Deep inside the ear, in a snail-shaped structure called the cochlea, thousands of tiny hair cells turn vibrations into signals that the brain reads as sound. Loud noise can bend or break these cells, and they do not grow back. When fewer signals arrive from the ear, the brain's hearing centers may become more active, as if turning up the volume to search for the missing input. Many researchers think this extra activity is what a person perceives as ringing.

(3) Noise is not the only cause. Earwax buildup, ear infections, certain medications, head injuries and the gradual hearing loss that comes with age can all produce tinnitus. Because the causes vary, anyone who develops ringing that does not go away, especially in one ear, is advised to have a hearing evaluation.

(4) There is no single treatment that silences tinnitus for everyone, but many people find ways to make it less bothersome. Hearing aids can help when hearing loss is present, because amplifying outside sounds gives the brain more to process. Sound generators that play soft background noise can make the ringing less noticeable, particularly at bedtime. Counseling approaches teach people to shift their attention away from the sound, which can reduce the distress it causes even when the sound itself does not change.

(5) Prevention is by far the wisest approach. Earplugs at concerts, earmuffs when using power tools, and keeping headphone volume at a moderate level all reduce the strain on the cochlea's hair cells. A brief period of ringing after a loud event is best treated as a warning: the ears were exposed to more sound than they could comfortably handle.

RC30.p:
(1) Falls are among the most frequently reported safety events in hospitals. Patients may be weak from illness, dizzy from new medications or unfamiliar with their surroundings, and a fall can turn a short stay into a long one. In 2022, a 300-bed community hospital decided to test whether a set of simple changes could reduce falls on its medical wards.

(2) Before the program began, the hospital recorded 4.2 falls for every 1,000 days that patients spent on those wards, a standard measure known as "patient days." Staff reviewed each fall from the previous year and found a pattern: more than half happened between midnight and 6 a.m., and most involved patients getting up alone to use the bathroom.

(3) The program addressed that pattern directly. Nurses and aides began hourly rounds during the night, asking each patient about pain, position and the need to use the toilet. Beds were lowered to their lowest height, call buttons were placed within reach, and patients judged to be at high risk received nonslip socks and a bed alarm that alerted staff when they began to stand.

(4) After twelve months, the fall rate on the medical wards had dropped to 2.9 per 1,000 patient days, a decline of about 31 percent. Falls that caused an injury fell from 19 the year before to 11. Night-shift staff also reported fewer calls for help that came after a patient was already out of bed.

(5) The hospital's report urged caution in reading these results. During the same year, the hospital added two nurses to the night shift on each medical ward, and the average age of admitted patients was slightly lower than in the year before. Either change could have contributed to the improvement. The authors also noted that the program was tried on one type of ward in one hospital. Even so, the report called the plan's low cost "an easy choice for any hospital that takes patient safety seriously."

RC31.p:
(1) A single blood donation takes about ten minutes, but the journey of that pint of blood has just begun when the donor leaves the chair. Within hours, the blood is on its way to a processing center, where it will be tested, separated and stored so that it can help as many as three patients.

(2) The first step is labeling. Each bag and its small sample tubes receive a matching bar code, which lets staff trace every product back to its donor without using the donor's name. The sample tubes go to a laboratory, where they are typed for blood group and screened for infections that can be passed on through transfusion, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

(3) While testing is under way, the bag itself is placed in a centrifuge, a machine that spins it at high speed. Spinning causes the parts of blood to settle into layers by weight. The heavy red blood cells sink to the bottom; the yellowish plasma, which is mostly water, rises to the top; and a thin middle layer holds platelets and white blood cells. Each layer is then pressed into its own attached bag.

(4) The three main products are stored in very different ways. Red cells are refrigerated and last about six weeks. Plasma is frozen and can be kept for up to a year. Platelets, which help blood clot, must be kept at room temperature and gently rocked, and they expire in about five to seven days. No product is released to a hospital until every test on its sample has come back clear; a unit with a positive result is discarded.

(5) Because platelets spoil so quickly, blood centers cannot stockpile them for emergencies. A trauma patient might need platelets from several donors in a single night, and patients receiving cancer treatment may need them regularly. For this reason, centers often call on donors who give platelets through a separate process that collects them directly.

RC32.t: Radon: The Gas You Cannot Sense
RC32.p:
(1) Radon is a radioactive gas that forms naturally when uranium in soil and rock breaks down. It has no color, odor or taste, so people cannot tell when they are breathing it. Outdoors, radon spreads into the air and stays at low levels. Indoors, it can collect, entering through cracks in foundations, gaps around pipes and other openings in the parts of a building that touch the ground.

(2) When radon is inhaled, tiny radioactive particles can lodge in the lining of the lungs and damage cells over time. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) ranks radon as the second leading cause of lung cancer in the United States after smoking, and the leading cause among people who have never smoked. The risk is greatest for smokers, because the two exposures together raise the danger far more than either one alone.

(3) Radon levels can differ sharply between neighboring houses, so the only way to know a home's level is to test it. The EPA recommends that homeowners take action when a test shows 4 picocuries per liter of air (pCi/L) or more. Do-it-yourself test kits are sold at hardware stores and usually cost less than $30.

(4) A recent county program shows what testing can reveal. Of 2,400 households that used free kits, 432, or 18 percent, had levels at or above 4 pCi/L. Many of those homes sat a few hundred feet from houses with low readings. Among the 150 high-reading households that went on to install a mitigation system, follow-up tests found that levels fell below 2 pCi/L in 141 homes.

(5) The most common mitigation system is a pipe and fan that draw radon from beneath the foundation and vent it above the roof. Installation typically costs about as much as other moderate home repairs. Given how little a test kit costs, skipping the test is a foolish gamble. Testing again after any major renovation, and every few years in any case, keeps the results current.

RC33.p:
(1) A kidney stone begins as something too small to see: a single crystal. The kidneys filter waste from the blood and flush it out in urine. When urine holds more of certain minerals, such as calcium and oxalate, than its fluid can keep dissolved, the extra minerals can crystallize. Over weeks or months, crystals can cling together and grow into a hard stone, sometimes as small as a grain of sand and sometimes larger than a pea.

(2) Many stones cause no trouble while they sit inside the kidney. The pain begins when a stone moves into the ureter, the narrow tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. The stone can block the flow of urine and stretch the tube, causing sharp pain in the back or side that often comes in waves and may spread toward the lower abdomen. Small stones usually pass on their own within a few weeks, while larger ones may need to be broken up with sound waves or removed with a thin scope.

(3) The most important risk factor is one people can control: how much fluid they drink. When a person takes in too little water, urine becomes concentrated, and the minerals in it are more likely to form crystals. Stones are more common in hot climates and in summer, when people lose more water through sweat. Diets high in salt also raise the risk, because extra sodium causes the kidneys to release more calcium into the urine.

(4) For people who have had one stone, the chance of forming another is high; about half develop another within ten years. Doctors commonly advise these patients to drink enough water to produce pale yellow urine and to limit salty foods. Surprisingly, most are not told to cut back on calcium-rich foods such as milk and yogurt. Calcium eaten with meals binds to oxalate in the digestive tract, so less oxalate reaches the kidneys. Cutting calcium can therefore raise, rather than lower, the risk for many people.

(5) Kidney stones are painful, but they are also among the more preventable problems that send people to the emergency room. A habit as simple as carrying a water bottle can make a real difference.

RC34.p:
(1) Every summer, our city issues heat warnings, opens cooling centers and urges residents to stay indoors. These steps save lives, but they treat extreme heat as an emergency that arrives without warning. It does not. Heat waves are now a predictable part of the season, and the city should treat shade as basic public health infrastructure, as important as clean water or safe sidewalks.

(2) The case begins with the numbers. Heat kills more Americans in a typical year than any other kind of extreme weather. Paved streets and rooftops absorb sunlight all day and release it at night, so city neighborhoods can stay several degrees warmer than the nearby countryside long after sunset. Studies of city surfaces have found that a sidewalk under a mature tree can be 20 degrees Fahrenheit or more cooler than one in full sun.

(3) Those cooler surfaces are not shared equally. Our own parks department's 2023 survey found that tree canopy covers 38 percent of the land in the city's northern neighborhoods but just 11 percent in the eastern districts, where more residents are older adults, work outdoors or live without air conditioning. In other words, the people least able to escape the heat are the ones walking on the hottest pavement.

(4) Critics argue that trees are expensive to water, that roots crack sidewalks, and that the money would be better spent on air-conditioned cooling centers. These are fair concerns, and each has an answer. Choosing drought-tolerant species and planting them in wider beds addresses most of the cost and damage. Cooling centers help the people who can reach them, while a shaded block protects everyone who walks it, including the bus rider waiting at a stop at 3 p.m.

(5) A tree planted this spring will not cast meaningful shade for perhaps ten years. That delay is exactly why the city council should fund a large planting program in the eastern districts now. Waiting for the next record-breaking summer to start would be a costly mistake.

RC35.p:
(1) In the 1890s, a French physician named Albert Calmette, working in what is now Vietnam, set out to find a treatment for cobra bites. Building on earlier work showing that animals could be made resistant to toxins, he injected animals with small amounts of venom and later used their blood to protect others. By 1895, he had produced one of the first antivenoms. More than a century later, the basic method he used remains in place.

(2) Production begins with venom. Trained handlers "milk" snakes by guiding their fangs over a covered container and gently pressing the venom glands. The venom is dried and stored until enough has been gathered. Next, a horse or sheep receives a series of injections, starting with a dose too small to harm it and slowly increasing over several months. The animal's immune system responds by making antibodies, proteins that latch onto the venom and block its effects.

(3) Once the animal's blood contains high levels of these antibodies, a portion of its blood is drawn, much as a person gives blood at a donation center. Laboratories separate the plasma and purify the antibodies, removing other proteins that might cause a reaction in patients. The finished product is often freeze-dried so that it can be stored for long periods without refrigeration, which matters in rural areas far from hospitals.

(4) An antivenom works against the venoms it was made from. A product made using one cobra species may do little against the bite of a different snake. To address this problem, many manufacturers combine venoms from several dangerous local species, producing a "polyvalent" antivenom that covers the snakes most likely to bite in a given region.

(5) Snakebite remains a serious problem in parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America, where it kills tens of thousands of people each year. In 2017, the World Health Organization added snakebite to its list of neglected tropical diseases. Because antivenom is costly to produce and is sold in relatively small amounts, some manufacturers have stopped making it, and shortages have followed in several countries.
